FULL VIEW
OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Explain the importance of negotiation skills in personal life and business life.
Discuss challenges associated with negotiating a medical employment contract.
Recognize important terms associated with medical employment contracts, managed care
contracts, and device company contracts.
Introduction

Introduction
A main concern of residents may be their first employment contract. This contract and
the negotiations that surround it likely will be the most inconsequential aspects of your
long career in orthopaedics. This lesson reviews a resident’s first contract for




NOTES

employment and emphasizes the many challenges that will require negotiation and
contracting skills.
All contracts are a memorialization of negotiations; however, not all negotiations, even
important ones, end in a contract.
Negotiations
Residents must train themselves in negotiation skills. One business skill that towers over all
others is being a skillful negotiator. Everything is a negotiation in business and personal life.
Whether negotiating a takeover of another orthopaedic group or negotiating for more block time,
the same skills are used.
Probable Negotiations
First job
Negotiating with a spouse/significant other, possibly on possible locations.
Terms of first contract
Often, this is a boilerplate contract; however, negotiation is possible.
Renewal contract
Clinical practice support (eg, medical assistant, administrative assistant, advanced practice
provider)
Research support, if in an academic setting
Clinic schedule
Operating room time
Call schedule
Device companies
Consulting contracts
Insurance companies
Responsibilities in the organization
Retirement options
Although these items are negotiable, not all negotiations result in contracts. Some negotiations
end in an understanding, a handshake, a general agreement, or group consensus. Conversely, all
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:48 AM
AAOS | Contracts and Negotiations
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003006
2/20

contracts are the result of a negotiation.
Everything Is Negotiable

Everything Is Negotiable
Everything is negotiable. All negotiating books state this; however, physicians frequently
do not believe this in certain situations. For example, a physician joins a group, and the
managing partner states that everyone has the same deal. That deal is memorialized in
your contract, and the managing partner states that, because of that, it is not negotiable.
This is completely wrong. Perhaps some items in the contract may be difficult to
negotiate because of fairness; however, every contingency likely was not counted on in
the contract for every situation. If a physician is an extraordinarily innovative individual
who plans to have patents and other forms of intellectual property, such issues may not
be in the contract or may not be written in your favor. The item may be completely
unimportant to every other partner but may be critically important to such a physician.
This is a clause such a physician would negotiate and likely win or on which a mutually
agreeable conclusion is reached.
Surgeons also should have a mindset that every deal needs to be negotiated. Physicians
can negotiate with the medical records department at a hospital with regard to when
charts are signed as easily as physicians can negotiate the number of patients they agree
to see per hour in clinic. Every item not negotiated is a lost opportunity.
Three Categories of Negotiations

Three Categories of Negotiations
Herb Cohen noted the following critical lessons in his classic book You Can Negotiate
Anything: How to Get Anything You Want.
The outcome of negotiations depends on an individual’s position related to three areas:
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:48 AM
AAOS | Contracts and Negotiations
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003006
3/20

Time
Information
Power
Time—If an individual is in a rush to get something done and the other party is not, then
a natural advantage exists for the party who has time.
Information—This likely is the most critical in a medical career, especially for those
employed by large groups, corporations, or health systems. Having information about
everything, including marketing budgets, salaries of ancillary staff, the individual who
controls block time, why the last surgeon who joined decided to leave, and more, puts a
physician in the best possible position to enter into negotiations. Make a list of every
piece of missing information concerning the specifics of that negotiation, and attempt to
get as much of that information as possible.
Power—Occasionally in a negotiation, an uneven power relationship exists. For example,
physicians may be negotiating with the sole owner of a practice they are part of. This
puts more power in the other party’s hands. Conversely, the physician may be a big
earner for the practice, which shifts some power. Surgeons should understand all the
features of power leverage in the relationship before entering a negotiation.
Negotiation as Personal but not Emotional
Negotiating is personal.
Develop a relationship.
Ask for exactly what you want.

Negotiation as Personal but not Emotional
Negotiations often affect individuals personally. Therefore, all negotiations should be
undertaken personally; however, they should not be undertaken emotionally. Emotions,
such as anger toward the tactics of the other person or feeling concern about the
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:48 AM
AAOS | Contracts and Negotiations
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003006
4/20

situation if desired terms are not attained, shifts attention away from the important
focus of a physician’s negotiation strategy.
Developing a Relationship

Developing a Relationship
A negotiation is about a relationship, whether it is a short-term or long-term
relationship. First, individuals like to deal with people they like. Second, this may not be
the last negotiation that occurs with this person or entity. In fact, most negotiations in
health care are recurring, and individuals remember poor behavior from previous
negotiations. Respect for the other side and their terms can be accomplished; however,
physicians can still have a firm negotiating stance.
Ask for the Order

Ask for the Order
One of the great failures of not achieving goals in a negotiation is failure to ask for
desired items. A person would never go into a restaurant and be unclear to the waiter
about what he or she wants for dinner. A person should ask for the order. The same
goes for negotiations—if an item is desired, then it should be placed on your list of
terms. Never assume the other party would never approve the item or that they would
be angry if it is requested. These are emotions that have no place in a negotiation.
Applicable Laws and Compliance Regulations
Understand the legal implications of all negotiations.
Negotiations start earlier than you think.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:48 AM
AAOS | Contracts and Negotiations
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003006
5/20


Applicable Laws and Compliance Regulations
Specifically in dealing with healthcare negotiations, surgeon must understand federal
and state regulations as they relate to the terms being negotiated. Some arrangements
are not legal in some states but are legal in other states. After terms are set, physicians
should check with their lawyer as to the legality of these terms in the jurisdictions in
which medicine will be practiced.
Beginnings of Negotiations

Beginnings of Negotiations
This is the least obvious and the most crucial tenets of this lesson. Many individuals
believe that a negotiation begins when people decide to make a deal with one another.
One side or the other likely predicted that the days of negotiation would occur and
began maneuvering to attain an advantage in these future negotiations. Knowledge of a
possible future negotiation allows physicians to gain competitive intelligence and key
financial information and sets a tone before the negotiation without the other side
knowing this is a tactic.
Three Columns of Negotiation Terms
Understand the following:
Terms that are dealbreakers
Terms you prefer
Terms you do not care about
Use your ranking of the terms to properly give concessions to get what you want.

Three Columns of Negotiation Terms
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:48 AM
AAOS | Contracts and Negotiations
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003006
6/20

In entering into a negotiation, all of a physician’s desired terms must be listed. These
may be related to compensation, termination clause, emergency call payment, or any
other desired items. In general, depending on the market and the current healthcare
environment, these terms differ in specifics but do not differ in that they must be
organized into three major categories:
Deal breakers: must have terms
Pluses/minuses: preferred terms that can be offered up in exchange for another term
Do not care: terms a physician does not care about
A simple example is shown in Table 1.
Table 1 The Three Columns of Negotiating Terms: A Sample List
Deal Breakers
Pluses/Minuses
Do Not Care
Restrictive covenant
Health benefits
On-call schedule
Termination clause
Block time
Retirement benefits
RVU compensation rules
Personal PA/NP
Personal secretary
Second contract terms
Salary range
NP = nurse practitioner, PA = physician assistant, RVU = relative value unit.
Courtesy of Ira H. Kirschenbaum, MD, Bronx, NY.
Only a physician and his or her lawyer know the terms listed in each category. In
negotiations, all these terms are presented as equally important. The person or entity
with which a physician is negotiating with does not know what terms are in each
category. Because concessions are almost always necessary in a negotiation, the goal is
to give concessions in the following order: Do not care items and then pluses/minuses
items. A term in the deal breaker category likely should not be conceded. Because the
other party does not know a physician’s priorities, giving a concession from the do not
care section may result in receiving a term in the high-priority categories.
Table 1 shows an example of the three columns of negotiating terms. The deal breakers
column lists items that physicians should seriously think about before giving up. The
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:48 AM
AAOS | Contracts and Negotiations
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003006
7/20

pluses/minuses column lists items that are perks; some items may be more important
than others and they should be placed in order in this column. The do not care column
lists items a physician is willing to concede in exchange for a higher priority item.
Win-Win Situation
Understand that both sides in a negotiation may have different priorities.
If both sides attain these priorities, that is called a win-win situation.
If you cannot negotiate your terms, understand your alternative to no negotiation (BATNA).
Be patient during a negotiation; the most important decisions are made in the last 5 minutes.
Do not depend on your lawyer to get your terms.
You can return to negotiate at any time.
Identify negotiating tactics.

Win-Win Situation
A term that tends to be overused is win-win. Both sides of a negotiation likely will use
this term at least once during a negotiation. The term refers to a final situation in which
both sides feel they have gained something from the negotiation or at least attained the
major terms they wanted. A win-win situation certainly can happen, especially if both
sides are honest and flexible on less important terms. This emphasizes the importance
of categorizing terms and knowing when and on what to give a concession.
A good example of a win-win is a situation in which a physician appears to lose
something for the short term to seal the negotiation; however, the physician wins in the
long term. For example, a physician invents a new device and starts a company to
design, manufacture, and distribute this device. The physician brings in a few partners
and owns 60% of the company. The physician is able to manufacture a prototype and
realizes that substantial capital is necessary for production and a distribution network is
not available. A large device company wants to buy the idea, bring it to the finish line,
and become the exclusive distributor of the product. The device company offers the
physician an initial lump sum and 6% of the gross sale of the product to complete buy
him or her out. The physician decides to give up any control of the product and take a
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:48 AM
AAOS | Contracts and Negotiations
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003006
8/20

smaller percentage of the profits; however, the physician achieves a financial windfall
with the large company behind him or her. In negotiating terms, this is known as having
a smaller piece of a bigger pie.
Walking Away and BATNA

Walking Away and BATNA
Physicians always need to be ready to walk away from a negotiation. This may not be
desirable. This may be a dream job; however, the dream may turn into a nightmare if
deal breaker terms are conceded. Walking away from a job, especially late in a
negotiation, is difficult. Therefore, every negotiation should be entered with a BATNA.
This is a term that was first used in the classic negotiating book Getting to Yes: Negotiating
Agreement Without Giving In by Roger Fisher and William Ury. BANTA stands for the best
alternative to a negotiated agreement.
Physicians who understand what their situation will be if a negotiated agreement cannot
be reached are in a strong position. This is because, in general, a negotiated agreement
that is worse than an individual’s BATNA should not be accepted. With employment
contracts this may be a difficult situation; however, many negotiations in which an
individual’s BATNA may be better than the results of a negotiation are possible.
The Last 5 Minutes

The Last 5 Minutes
Negotiations can take a long time. Do not be in a rush to make concessions or agree to
terms early in the negotiation. The first part of the negotiation is an assessment of the
person or parties of the deal. Attempting to decide who in the room, or out of the room,
is the ultimate decision maker. Eventually, the physician should want to be in the room
with that person.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:48 AM
AAOS | Contracts and Negotiations
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003006
9/20

Regardless, physicians should attempt to not give concessions or clues to their position
early in the negotiation. In fact, many state that everything happens in the last 5
minutes. Perhaps not exactly the last 5 minutes but certainly toward the end of the
negotiation. This is the time during which a physician needs to be sharpest and most
cautious. Often, an enormous amount of pressure exists to seal the deal with just one
more concession at the eleventh hour. That rarely is the case. Physicians should hold
their line to the very end.
Negotiating and Your Lawyer

Negotiating and Your Lawyer
The lawyer a physician hires to do his or her contract does not have the negotiating skills
a physician needs. Lawyers have contracting skills; however, these skills are completely
separate skills. Lawyers can possibly advise a physician on the terms developed with
valued advisors; however, but that is all it is—advice. A lawyer’s main role is to ensure a
physician is protected, legally, in all aspects of the expression of his or her negotiating
terms that are set forth in the contract.
Return to Negotiate

Return to Negotiate
Athletes renegotiate arrangements; so can physicians. For example, a physician
negotiates for an extra block day a week at an ambulatory surgery center. Then, the
physician’s volume grows. The physician goes back to the negotiating table. The other
side may say that this was just negotiated; however, things change. Physicians should
always be ready to return to the negotiating table.
Identification of Tactics
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:48 AM
AAOS | Contracts and Negotiations
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003006
10/20


Identification of Tactics
Frequently, physicians may notice that the individual on the other side of the negotiation
is using some of the tactics recommended in this lesson. Good or bad, after a tactic is
recognized, it can be called out. This erodes the other individual’s negotiating position.
Contracts
Overview
Contracts follow a negotiation.
Learn to develop term sheets.
Read all parts of every contract, including the fine print.

Overview
Contracts are nothing more than the legal memorialization of a negotiation. Without a
negotiation, a physician should not even consider signing a contract. Not all negotiations
lead to contracts. Sometimes negotiations lead to a handshake agreement or a general
consensus moving forward; however, all contracts had negotiations before they existed.
Term Sheets

Term Sheets
Based on knowledge already collected (eg, from public sources, such as an Internet
search, and advice from colleagues, family, and friends) physicians will develop a term
sheet based on desired items in a contract. Term sheet—A term sheet is an organized
and prioritized list of desired terms in a contract.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:48 AM
AAOS | Contracts and Negotiations
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003006
11/20

If the contract has already been received, the term sheet collects and organizes the
items a physician wants changed in the contract. This is an important step that is a
physician’s responsibility. The terms should be placed in the three-column grid: deal
breakers, pluses/minuses, do not care.
Writing Terms and Finding a Lawyer

Writing Terms and Finding a Lawyer
After development of the term sheet, physicians should retain legal counsel and give
them this term sheet. The lawyer will read the term sheet and add more terms that the
physician may have forgotten or not considered. An important exercise in achieving a
quality contract is thinking of terms and incorporating a lawyer’s terms into the contract.
This does not diminish the lawyer’s role in the process; instead, it enhances it.
Usually in a medical contract situation, after these terms are developed, the lawyer goes
to bat for the physician. Physicians have not been absolved from negotiating. The other
party, who may be a future partner or partners, also will want to negotiate with the
physician. Physicians should work closely and in tandem with their lawyer.
Fine Print

Fine Print
Often, medical employment contracts do not include much fine print; however, fine print
is included in managed care contracts, consulting contracts, and contracts in which
physicians determine pricing for medical devices. The power of this fine print should not
be underestimated. Often, all kinds of restrictions and exclusions are in these areas.
Medical Employment Contracts
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:48 AM
AAOS | Contracts and Negotiations
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003006
12/20


Medical Employment Contracts
Read your medical employment contract in a methodic manner.
Leave no stone unturned; every part of a contract needs to be perceived as
negotiable.
Read the Contract in the Following Manner
Read the contract all the way through once.
Highlight obvious problem issues.
Sequentially focus on the sections in the following order:
Termination clauses: what physicians should strive for
Suggestion: at will termination rather than for cause termination
If things are simply not working out, a physician may want to simply leave and
not have unsubstantiated claims filed against him or her for removal.
Release of any restrictive covenant if the other party terminates or does not renew
or if the other party change a second contract, causing the physician to need to
leave
Strive for 6 months’ notification on termination. At the time the other party asks
the physician to leave, the other party owes the physician 6 months minus the
time the physician left. If the other party asks the physician to leave immediately,
then the physician gets 6 months of pay.
The physician must have access to all his or her medical records on demand after
he or she leaves.
The physician needs contact information for his or her surgical patients.
The physician’s forwarding telephone number must be given if any patient calls
and asks for the physician by name.
Compensation
Is it what was expected?
Is it realistic to attain?
Does the market and practice history support revenue/income assumptions?
Contract: first versus second
Is this the final contract? If not, what are the terms of the second contract? The
second contract is more important.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:48 AM
AAOS | Contracts and Negotiations
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003006
13/20

Is the second contract mentioned?
Does everyone in the group have the same second contract?
Ancillary income
What is the current status of EVERY physician in the practice?
What is the income every physician in the practice receives from any corporations
related to the practice of medicine and ancillary services (such as the group or
parties in the group owning physical therapy, imaging, or an ambulatory surgery
center)?
Is there is a buy-in? If so, why? Negotiate this heavily.
Clauses for audits by individuals of the physician’s choice and transparency
Intellectual property that a physician develops—Ensure all intellectual property is
the property of the physician even if company/hospital resources are used.
Definitions of outside activities of income and assurance that the physician keeps all
this money
Income for which a medical degree is not necessary
Independent medical examinations
Device royalties and consulting
Can the physician decide to accept certain insurances? Physicians do not want to be
the only in-network physician if all the other physicians are out-of-network.
What happens on retirement?
This list includes many variables; reviewing every example is impossible; however,
physicians should concentrate on the categories listed.
Managed Care Contracts
Managed care contracts should be taken seriously.
Managed care contracts are just as negotiable as any other contract.
Negotiate the terms that are important to you.

Managed Care Contracts
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:48 AM
AAOS | Contracts and Negotiations
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003006
14/20

Managed care contracts are not boilerplate agreements. Although they may involve
large, multinational corporations, certain terms can be negotiated. Areas of opportunity
include the following:
Physician responsibilities in the audit process.
Some of these processes may be draconian. For example, records on demand, unlimited
records, and phone call records may be requested. Physicians can negotiate a fee for all
these events.
Fees for certain procedures
Physicians likely do not perform every procedure in the Current Procedural Terminology
list. Insurance companies have been known to carve out increased reimbursement for a
select number of Current Procedural Terminology codes to keep a physician in-network.
Procedures that are experimental/investigational
This is an important issue. For example, physicians who are proponents of
orthobiologics may want to negotiate these into their contract from the start as not
being in this category.
Manner in which medical necessity is determined
Ask to see all guidelines that determine decision making for approval and medical
necessity.
The structure of denials and appeals processes
Ensure a time-limit exists for the appeals process and potential arbitration. Equally
important is a physician’s ability to request a peer-to-peer with an orthopaedic surgeon
(not just another medical physician) at any point in time.
Whether authorization is necessary for certain procedures
Many surgeons rarely are denied authorization for procedures. Therefore, physicians
can negotiate requirements to not obtain authorization for certain procedures.
Whether procedures decided on during surgery are paid.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:48 AM
AAOS | Contracts and Negotiations
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003006
15/20

At times during a procedure, unexpected procedures occur that are billable. Contracts
must have a provision for this.
Device Company Contracts
Two types of device company contracts
Consulting/designing surgeon
Prices for devices for your ambulatory surgical center or hospital
Ensure your practice allows for consulting and designing surgeon contracts.
Understand all the terms in the agreement.
Many other terms besides price exist in device company contracts.

Device Company Contracts
Orthopaedic surgeons commonly enter into contracts with device companies during
their career. Such contracts primarily include the following:
Consultant or royalty agreement
Negotiating device prices on behalf of an ambulatory surgery center or hospital
The aforementioned negotiation principles also apply in negotiating with a device
company. Surgeons should be aware of important contract issues.
In agreeing to consult for a device company, physicians should ensure that their contract
with their current employer allows for such consultation. Good contracts would have
resulted in intellectual property and outside consulting being removed from the table so
that the employer cannot make decisions regarding a physician’s ability to move ahead
with consulting or attain any part of a physician’s consulting compensation.
With any device manufacturer or vendor in the healthcare space, ensure a contract is in
place. Never rely on e-mail agreements or letters of intent. These entities not protect the
physician on the terms that he or she desires. In addition, state and federal regulations
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:48 AM
AAOS | Contracts and Negotiations
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003006
16/20

govern the relationships between physicians and device companies and other healthcare
vendors. E-mails may be problematic in that intentions and terms rarely are clearly
defined. Physicians should select a lawyer familiar with these regulations. Physicians
should not assume that the company lawyers properly configured the contractual
relationship to protect them.
Exercise caution in entering into these agreements; do so only if real value in the form of
intellectual property special knowledge can be offered. Anything else may be perceived
as suspicious and raise red flags and may be unlawful and unethical.
Contracts related to device prices have features in them that do not only include the
price of the implants. Device companies attempt to place some common terms in the
language of the contract that generally are not in a physician’s favor.
Minimal Volume
This is a clause that affords the physician a price based on his or her volume. This seems
somewhat reasonable. If 1,000 shirts are bought from a manufacturer, the price is less
per shirt than if five shirts are bought. However, in the device company situation, selling
one joint versus 100 joints is not more expensive. Volume clause discounts must be
removed so surgeons simply can get the best price.
Gag Clause
Some contracts include language that does not allow the physician to share the price
with others outside the health system. Some physicians may be fine with such clauses;
however, surgeons should be aware that this clause is enforceable. From the perspective
of proponents of a transparent healthcare system, such clauses are bad for health care
overall.
Consignment
Consignment is an arrangement in which a company puts product on the shelf and the
physician pays for the product if he or she uses it. The key terms to consider in this
arrangement include the following:
Ensure the minimum levels necessary are present.
Be careful about shipping charges. If one product costs $200 and a replacement
involves $75 shipping charges, no benefit exists. Consider a clause that states that no
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:48 AM
AAOS | Contracts and Negotiations
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003006
17/20

shipping charges will apply if a representative is present in the room or who visits the
hospital on a regular basis.
The responsibility for missing consignment items should not fall on the physician.
Despite locking up items, items may mysteriously go missing. If a physician and a
company agree that items have been properly locked up, all missing inventory is the
company’s responsibility.
Boxed Items
Occasionally, one item that comes in a box of 10 is necessary. Ensure charges are only
for item usage. Do not buy the box.
Expiration Exclusion
With an expiration exclusion, the company is responsible for checking expiration dates
and substituting items on a physician’s shelf, whether bought or on consignment, free of
charge, that are close to or past expiration dates.
Obsolescence Clause
In case the company introduces a new and improved product for a produced already
purchased, ensure the contract states that the old inventory or product is traded out for
the new inventory or product at the same price for the life of that contract. This includes
large capital expenses, such as microscopes and robotics; however, in such cases, the
clause usually includes a time-period limitation. For example, physicians may request
that within 5 years of purchase of a product, if the next version comes out, a free or
prorated trade-out is received.
Summary
Negotiations and contracting are part art and part science. Negotiations will occur more
frequently than imagined throughout a physician’s career.
